title: 5 European countries want to start deporting migrants to Rwanda, despite concerns from human rights groups
summary: Five European countries have embarked on a deal with Rwanda to take in migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected. They are hoping the scheme acts as a deterrent, but a similar plan in Britain…

blocks.text: World·Analysis

Five European countries have embarked on a deal with Rwanda to take in migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected. They are hoping the scheme acts as a deterrent, but a similar plan in Britain was quashed after the court called it unlawful.
Countries working with Rwanda to set up 'return hub' for migrants who don't have legal right to remain in EU

In one of his first acts as Britain's prime minister, Keir Starmer in 2024 quashed the U.K. government's controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, saying it was "dead and buried before it started."
Now, five European countries are trying to resurrect a similar scheme.

Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced Monday that they are working with Rwanda to set up a "return hub" for migrants who do not have the legal right to remain in the European Union.

"We need to take back control of our borders," said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen during a joint news conference in Vienna. "What we are pushing for is a more sustainable and, I will also say, a more orderly asylum and migration system."
Those sent to Rwanda will be given the chance to integrate and settle there or another nation that grants them the legal right to stay — or return to their home country.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at a joint news conference that the EU countries' Rwanda deportation hub plan would be a 'game changer' for illegal migration. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
Mounting political pressure

The plan, which some EU officials have dubbed a "game changer," is part of a hardening stance toward asylum seekers. It comes as many European governments face growing pressure from voters and rival far-right political parties to show they can control migration.
In September, a regional election victory by Germany’s far-right, anti-immigration party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), was widely seen as a symbol of changing public sentiment toward migration.

Over the past few years, asylum claims in Europe have been dropping, and experts point to a combination of factors, including changes in government policy and the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in Syria in 2024. In 2023, there were more than a million first-time asylum applications. Last year, the annual figure dropped to just under 670,000, according to data from the European Union.

Migrants board a coast guard boat from a Frontex vessel, to be transferred to the port of Kaloi Limenes, following a rescue operation on the island of Crete, Greece, on Nov. 9. (Stefanos Rapanis/Reuters)
Britain's failed experiment
When Britain first unveiled its Rwanda partnership in 2022, then-prime minister Boris Johnson pitched it as necessary to stop boats full of asylum seekers from crossing the English Channel.
The year prior, there were nearly 50,000 asylum claims in the U.K.

Under the British plan, people could be sent to Rwanda while British authorities processed their asylum claims. Under the proposed European arrangement, the east-central African nation would only take in those whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who cannot be sent back to their home countries because of a lack of co-operation.

For Rwanda, proponents argue that the agreement presents an economic opportunity, and European officials are framing the country as an ideal place for a "second chance." Critics dispute that characterization, arguing Rwanda has a track record of repression. Amnesty International said that without scrutiny the Rwanda deal could become a "black hole for human rights."

Britain's then-home secretary Suella Braverman, left, and Rwanda's then-minister of infrastructure Ernest Nsabimana, right, lay bricks at a housing development for migrants in the Rwandan capital Kigali on March 19, 2023. Britain eventually scrapped a controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda. (The Associated Press)
In a joint statement, 47 organizations urged the countries to scrap the Rwanda plan, arguing there are insufficient legal safeguards and no monitoring system to eliminate the risk of rights abuses.
In 2025 — two years after Britain's Supreme Court ruled the U.K.'s Rwanda plan unlawful — the U.S. struck its own deal with the country to accept up to 250 migrants.
No hard numbers

When European officials unveiled their agreement during Monday's news conference in Vienna, they said they hope to send the first people to Rwanda by the end of 2027, though they did not specify how many people in total would be sent there.

The five countries are billing the plan as a pilot project, insisting it will act as a deterrent to prevent people from travelling — sometimes thousands of kilometres — to reach Europe in the first place.

"As everybody knows, criminal organizations are making billions of euros on human smuggling, and too many lives are lost at sea," said Frederiksen. "We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders."
In her speech, Frederiksen said some European leaders have been working toward this kind of initiative for "eight or nine years."

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta says he believes that under the 'return hub' plan, asylum seekers in Europe may opt to return to their countries of origin without going through Rwanda at all. He added that Kigali was not planning for 'thousands' of people to stay in the east-central African nation. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
New EU rule

The announcement of the Rwanda hub comes a month and a half after the Council of the European Union greenlit a new policy, the EU Return Regulation, which opened the door to setting up migrant hubs outside Europe.
The rules stipulate that unaccompanied minors cannot be deported and that hubs can only be created in countries that respect "international human rights and the principles of international law."
Clémentine de Montjoye, a senior researcher in the Africa division at Human Rights Watch, called the plan "utterly deplorable," in part because of what she calls a stunning contradiction.

Europe has repeatedly voiced concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record and its support for M23, an armed group accused of committing war crimes in the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
De Montjoye pointed out that Germany even reduced its aid to Rwanda last year because of its role in the conflict, which has displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

A bicycle taxi driver looks on while waiting for customers at a busy junction near a market in Kigali, on July 16, 2024. The east African nation is set to host a deportation hub for failed asylum seekers from five European countries. (Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images)
Now, Germany and four other countries are trying to frame Rwanda as a land of opportunity.

"The question is: What kind of due diligence has been done by these five countries?" De Montjoye told CBC News from Nairobi, Kenya. "It's very concerning that the risk of human rights harms are being kind of swept under the carpet in order to present an image of coming up with solutions."
'Fig leaf' of deterrence

Outlining the motivations for creating the hub, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said European countries are hampered because countries of origin often do not co-operate when it comes to taking back rejected asylum seekers.
According to statistics from the Mixed Migration Centre, which operates under the Danish Refugee Council, only one in five people ordered to leave Europe actually do so.

A demonstrator holds a placard reading 'Stop EU-Rwanda-deal,' on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development on Monday in Vienna. (Radek Mica/AFP/Getty Images)
Roberto Forin, the centre's deputy director, says there is a need to manage migration in a more orderly way, but believes the Rwanda deal will act only as a "fig leaf" rather than a real deterrent.
He says smugglers will adapt, and asylum seekers who feel they have no alternative will continue to make risky journeys, even if the odds of being allowed to stay are lower.
"This is more about politics than migration policy," he told CBC News from Vienna. "Governments, actually across the political spectrum, have made a tough border as part of their promises to voters."
